title: Knowledge Check 12 - Lessons 56-62
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 56-62 - Best Fit Solutions. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A solution generates a large document inside an OmniScript and users report timeouts. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the OmniScript timeout to the maximum
Generate the document asynchronously and have the script confirm submission
Reduce the document size by removing required fields
Move the document generation to a FlexCard
questions.explanation: Generating the document asynchronously lets the OmniScript confirm submission and return control, which removes the synchronous wait and the timeout. Increasing the timeout only delays the failure. Removing required fields changes the business output. A FlexCard is a display component and does not generate documents.

questions.question: An architect is designing for a solution that will grow from hundreds to millions of records. Which practice best supports scalability?
options: Return full result sets so no data is ever missing
Keep queries selective and bounded, and cache read-mostly reference data
Run all work synchronously so results are always current
Store all external data in custom settings
questions.explanation: Selective and bounded queries plus cached reference data keep the solution within limits as data grows. Returning full result sets will hit row limits at scale. Running all work synchronously blocks users and does not scale. Custom settings are for configuration, not for storing large external datasets.

questions.question: A long-running Integration Procedure blocks the user's browser while it completes. What is the correct approach?
options: Keep it synchronous so the user sees the final result
Move the heavy work to asynchronous processing and let the script confirm submission
Duplicate the IP logic inside the OmniScript
Reduce the IP to a single Data Raptor
questions.explanation: Moving the heavy work to asynchronous processing lets the script confirm submission and return control, which is the scalable pattern. Keeping it synchronous preserves the block. Duplicating the logic adds maintenance without fixing the wait. A single Data Raptor cannot perform the external orchestration the IP does.

questions.question: An OmniScript needs to load a single account record by ID and display a few fields. What is the best fit?
options: An Integration Procedure that calls an external system
A Data Raptor that loads the account by ID
A FlexCard that queries the account
A scheduled Apex job that caches the account
questions.explanation: A Data Raptor is the direct, light way to load a single record by ID into the OmniScript's JSON. An Integration Procedure adds a server round trip for a simple local read. A FlexCard is a display component, not a data source for an OmniScript. A scheduled job is for background work, not an on-demand load.

questions.question: The same multi-source aggregation is needed by three OmniScripts and a FlexCard. Where should the logic live?
options: Duplicated inside each OmniScript
In a single shared Integration Procedure
In a Data Raptor inside one script
In a custom setting that stores the result
questions.explanation: A single shared Integration Procedure centralizes the aggregation so all consumers reuse one tested artifact. Duplicating it in each script creates drift. A Data Raptor inside one script is not shared. A custom setting stores configuration, not a live aggregation result.

questions.question: An OmniScript must save a parent record and several child records that must all succeed together. What is the best approach?
options: A save Data Raptor that writes the parent only
An Integration Procedure that orchestrates the multi-record save with error handling
A separate Data Raptor for each record with no coordination
A FlexCard that submits the records
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure can orchestrate the multi-record save and handle errors so a partial write does not leave the data inconsistent. A Data Raptor writing only the parent loses the children. Separate uncoordinated Data Raptors risk partial writes. A FlexCard is a display component and does not orchestrate saves.

questions.question: An architect is tracing a data element through an OmniScript and finds it is fetched but never displayed or saved. What should be done?
options: Keep it in the fetch in case it is needed later
Remove it from the fetch to reduce waste
Move it to a separate Integration Procedure
Store it in a custom setting
questions.explanation: A data element that is fetched but never used is waste, and removing it from the fetch reduces bandwidth, memory, and query budget. Keeping it in case it is needed later is speculative and inefficient. Moving it to a separate IP adds a round trip for unused data. A custom setting is for configuration, not for unused fetched data.

questions.question: A save operation writes a record even when none of its fields changed. What is the best improvement?
options: Write the record anyway to keep it simple
Design the save to write only the records and fields that changed
Add more fields to the save so it is more complete
Move the save to a FlexCard
questions.explanation: Writing only what changed avoids redundant writes, which waste time and trigger unnecessary triggers and workflows. Writing anyway is the inefficiency being fixed. Adding more fields makes the problem worse. A FlexCard is a display component and does not perform saves.

questions.question: A complex transformation must produce identical results for three OmniScripts. Where should it live?
options: Duplicated inside each OmniScript
In a single shared Integration Procedure
In the browser's JavaScript for each script
In a custom label that stores the output
questions.explanation: A single shared Integration Procedure guarantees identical results and is written and tested once. Duplicating it in each script risks drift. Browser JavaScript duplicated per script has the same drift problem. A custom label stores text, not a transformation result.

questions.question: A team is about to edit an OmniScript directly in production to fix a quick issue. What is the correct governance response?
options: Allow it because it is fast and declarative
Reject it and require the change to go through a sandbox and a deployment gate
Allow it but log the change manually
Allow it only for Integration Procedures
questions.explanation: Direct production edits bypass review, testing, and rollback, so the correct response is to reject it and require the change to flow through a sandbox and a deployment gate. Allowing it, even with manual logging, still lacks the controlled process. Restricting the exception to Integration Procedures does not address the risk for OmniScripts.

questions.question: An architect is defining the test plan for a new Integration Procedure that writes to an external system. What must the plan cover?
options: Only the happy path
External calls, payloads, and failure handling, plus the security context
Only the build, since it is declarative
Only the OmniScript that calls it
questions.explanation: An Integration Procedure that writes externally must be tested for its external calls, payloads, and failure handling, and for its security context, because those are where it can fail or expose data. Testing only the happy path misses the error cases. Testing only the build ignores behavior. Testing only the calling OmniScript ignores the IP's own behavior.

questions.question: A team wants to apply the same review depth to every OmniStudio artifact. What is the problem with this approach?
options: It is too strict for low-risk artifacts and too light for high-risk ones
It is the only fair way to govern
It makes deployments faster
It eliminates the need for version control
questions.explanation: A one-size review depth either overburdens low-risk artifacts or underprotects high-risk ones, so the process is not proportionate to risk. It is not the only fair way; proportionate governance is more effective. It does not make deployments faster, and it does not replace version control.

questions.question: A team is changing a label on an OmniScript and a change to an Integration Procedure that writes to an external system. How should the change process treat them?
options: Identically, with the same approval chain
Proportionately, with lighter review for the label and full scrutiny for the IP
The label needs no record, the IP needs full review
Neither needs review because both are declarative
questions.explanation: The change process should be proportionate to risk: a cosmetic label change gets lighter review, while a change to an external-writing IP gets full scrutiny. Treating them identically either overburdens the simple case or underprotects the risky one. The label still needs a record, so the third option is wrong. Declarative artifacts still need review, so the last option is wrong.

questions.question: An artifact's documentation describes it as it was three releases ago. What is the risk?
options: None, documentation is optional
The team trusts a record that is wrong and makes a change based on it
It makes the artifact faster
It replaces the need for version control
questions.explanation: Stale documentation misleads the next change because the team trusts a record that no longer matches the artifact. Documentation is not optional, so the first option is wrong. It does not make the artifact faster, and it does not replace version control.

questions.question: What should the documentation standard for a Data Mapper or Integration Procedure cover?
options: Only the artifact's name
The fields it reads and writes, the external systems it calls, and the JSON format it exchanges
Only the owner's name
Only the date it was created
questions.explanation: The data contract, including the fields read and written, the external systems called, and the JSON format, is what lets another team integrate safely and makes a change's impact visible. The name, owner, and creation date alone do not describe the artifact's behavior.

questions.question: An architect is starting a new solution and the business has not yet agreed on what it needs. What should be built first?
options: The physical model with objects and fields
The conceptual model in business language with the stakeholders
The OmniScript so the team can see it working
The Integration Procedure for the data flow
questions.explanation: The conceptual model is the contract with the business and should be built first in business language, because jumping to objects and fields forces technology decisions before the business agrees on what it needs. The physical model, OmniScript, and Integration Procedure all depend on that agreement.

questions.question: In which model does the architect decide whether an address is its own entity or part of an account?
options: Conceptual Model
Logical Model
Physical Model
None, it is a business decision only
questions.explanation: The Logical Model is where the data structure is decided, including whether an address is its own entity or part of an account. The Conceptual Model stays in business language without that structure. The Physical Model implements the decision already made. It is a data-structure decision, not only a business one.

questions.question: A platform constraint, such as a relationship limit, is discovered while building the physical model. What should the architect do?
options: Ignore it and build anyway
Raise it back to the logical and conceptual levels and adjust the design
Only document it in the physical model
Move the data to a custom setting
questions.explanation: A platform constraint discovered in the physical model must be raised back to the logical and conceptual levels so the design can adjust, keeping the models aligned. Ignoring it ships a broken model. Documenting it only in the physical model leaves the other models out of sync. A custom setting is not a substitute for a relationship.

questions.question: A business concept is a customer, and the solution needs the standard reporting and integration that come with it. What is the best object choice?
options: A custom object named Customer
The standard Account object
A custom setting
A custom metadata type
questions.explanation: A customer maps to the standard Account object, which brings the built-in reporting, integration, and familiarity the solution needs. A custom object duplicates the standard one and splits the data. A custom setting and a custom metadata type are for configuration, not for customer records.

questions.question: A business concept, such as a product configuration, has no clean standard object and the standard objects would force compromises. What is the best choice?
options: Force it into a standard object anyway
Create a custom object that matches the requirement
Store it in a custom label
Put it in a custom setting
questions.explanation: When a concept has no clean standard home and standard objects would force compromises, a custom object gives the team the shape it needs without the baggage. Forcing it into a standard object creates workarounds. A custom label and a custom setting are for configuration, not for transactional records.

questions.question: An architect is choosing between a lookup and a master-detail relationship for related records. What should drive the decision?
options: The default, which is always master-detail
The cascade, sharing, and reporting needs of the relationship
The number of fields on the object
The name of the object
questions.explanation: The choice between lookup and master-detail should be driven by the cascade, sharing, and reporting needs, because master-detail cascades deletes and controls access while a lookup is more flexible. The default is not always master-detail. Field count and object name do not determine the relationship type.
